title: Stacks, Queues and Ring Buffers

sections.heading: The ADTs and Their Invariants
sections.body:
A **stack** is a sequence $S=\langle s_1,\dots,s_n\rangle$ accessed only at one end, the *top* $s_n$: `push(x)` appends, `pop()` removes and returns $s_n$, and `top()` peeks without removing. The only invariant is **last-in-first-out (LIFO)** order — pop must always return the most recently pushed element that has not yet been popped.

A **queue** is the same sequence with the two operations split across opposite ends: `enqueue(x)` appends at the *tail* $s_n$, `dequeue()` removes from the *head* $s_1$. This is **first-in-first-out (FIFO)** order. Both ADTs expose `is_empty()`; bounded implementations also need `is_full()`.

Neither ADT mandates a representation, and CLRS's chapter on elementary data structures gives the two baseline realizations side by side: a bounded array with a `top` index for the stack, and a bounded array with separate `head`/`tail` indices for the queue (Figures 10.1-10.2), alongside the general dynamic-set linked-list machinery it also uses for lists (Figures 10.3-10.6). Every practical stack or queue is one of these two families, or a hybrid — and the representation invariant that has to be re-established after every operation is purely about the indices or pointers, never about the values: `top` (or `size`) must always equal the true number of live elements, and `head`/`tail` must always denote exactly the occupied range.

sections.heading: Array and Linked Representations
sections.body:
The array stack keeps elements in `a[0..top-1]`; `push` writes `a[top]` and increments `top`, `pop` decrements `top` and returns `a[top]`. If the array is fixed-size, both are $O(1)$ but can fail (overflow/underflow); if it is a growable array that doubles capacity when full, `push` is $O(1)$ **amortized** because the total copying cost across $n$ pushes is $O(n)$ (each element is copied $O(1)$ times on average over a geometric sequence of resizes), even though a single resizing push costs $\Theta(n)$ in the **worst case**.

The linked stack pushes and pops at the **head** of a singly linked list: `push` allocates a node, sets its `next` to the old head, and updates head — $O(1)$ worst case, no amortization needed, because the operation never touches more than one existing node.

A linked **queue** cannot use the same trick at both ends: `dequeue` naturally removes the head, but `enqueue` must append at the *opposite* end. Without an explicit `tail` pointer, finding the last node to append after costs $O(n)$ per enqueue; keeping a maintained `tail` pointer (updated by every enqueue, and reset to `NULL` when the last node is removed) restores $O(1)$ for both ends.

Arrays and linked nodes also differ in memory behavior: array elements are contiguous, so sequential pushes/pops stream through one or two cache lines with no pointer chasing and no per-element allocator overhead, while a linked node pays for a separate heap allocation and at least one extra pointer word, and successive nodes are not guaranteed to be adjacent in memory — traversal (rare for stacks/queues, common for iteration) can incur a cache miss per node.

sections.heading: Ring Buffers: Head, Tail and the Full-vs-Empty Ambiguity
sections.body:
A **ring buffer** (circular buffer) is a fixed-capacity array of size $C$ used as a queue: `head` indexes the oldest element, `tail` indexes the next free slot, and both wrap around modulo $C$ — `tail = (tail + 1) % C` on enqueue, `head = (head + 1) % C` on dequeue. This gives $O(1)$ worst-case enqueue/dequeue with no allocation, which is why ring buffers are the default queue inside interrupt handlers and lock-free single-producer/single-consumer pipes.

The classic trap: with only `head` and `tail`, the state `head == tail` is ambiguous — it means *empty* if nothing has been written since the pointers last coincided, but *full* if $C$ elements have been enqueued without a dequeue. Three standard fixes disambiguate it:

1. **Explicit count.** Track a separate `size` field, incremented on enqueue and decremented on dequeue; `head == tail` is read only together with `size == 0` or `size == C`.
2. **Wasted slot.** Only ever allow $C-1$ live elements; the buffer is full exactly when `(tail + 1) % C == head`, so `head == tail` unambiguously means empty. Simpler, costs one slot of capacity.
3. **Sticky flag.** A boolean set on the enqueue that makes `tail` catch up to `head`, cleared on the next dequeue.

When $C$ is a power of two, `% C` is replaced by `& (C - 1)`, a single AND instead of a division — the technique behind lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffers used in device drivers and high-throughput network I/O.

sections.heading: Queue from Two Stacks: Amortized Analysis
sections.body:
A FIFO queue can be built from two LIFO stacks, `in` and `out`. `enqueue(x)` always pushes `x` onto `in`. `dequeue()` pops from `out` if `out` is non-empty; otherwise it transfers every element of `in` onto `out` (popping each from `in`, pushing it onto `out`) and then pops from `out`. The transfer reverses `in` exactly once, and since `in` itself already reversed the enqueue order once, the two reversals cancel: elements leave `out` in the same order they entered `in`, so FIFO order is preserved. Each element is pushed onto `in` once, moved to `out` at most once, and popped from `out` once — at most four primitive stack operations over its whole lifetime — so any sequence of $m$ queue operations does $O(m)$ primitive work in total, i.e. $O(1)$ **amortized** per operation, even though a single `dequeue` that triggers a transfer of $k$ elements costs $\Theta(k)$ in the **worst case**.

The potential method makes this precise. Define $\Phi = 2\,|\text{in}|$ (twice the number of elements currently sitting in `in`, since each will eventually cost one pop-from-`in` plus one push-to-`out` when transferred). For `enqueue`, actual cost $1$, $\Delta\Phi = +2$, amortized cost $3$. For `dequeue` with `out` non-empty, actual cost $1$, $\Delta\Phi = 0$, amortized cost $1$. For `dequeue` that transfers $k$ elements, actual cost $2k+1$, $\Delta\Phi = -2k$, amortized cost $1$. Every case is $O(1)$, matching the aggregate bound; the worked example below traces the potential through a concrete sequence.

sections.heading: Expression Evaluation with a Stack
sections.body:
Postfix (reverse Polish) evaluation is the canonical stack application: scan the expression left to right; push each operand; on an operator, pop the top two operands, apply the operator, and push the result. For `"3 4 + 2 *"`, the trace is push 3 → push 4 → pop 4, pop 3, push $3+4=7$ → push 2 → pop 2, pop 7, push $7 \times 2 = 14$; the stack holds exactly one value, $14$, at the end. Because each operator consumes exactly the two most recently produced values, order matters for non-commutative operators: for `a b -`, the top of the stack (popped first) is the **second** operand $b$, and the result is $a - b$, not $b - a$.

Converting infix to postfix (or evaluating infix directly) uses a second stack for **pending operators**, following the shunting-yard idea: operands go straight to the output; an operator is pushed only after popping and emitting every operator already on the stack with strictly greater or equal precedence (respecting associativity); parentheses push on `(` and, on `)`, pop and emit until the matching `(` is discarded. The invariant maintained is that the operator stack is always sorted by precedence from bottom (lowest) to top (highest), which is exactly what lets a single pop-and-emit loop restore it after every token.

sections.heading: Variants, Trade-offs and Real Systems
sections.body:
Operating-system kernels lean on exactly these two ADTs for bookkeeping — Silberschatz et al.'s kernel-data-structures chapter groups lists, stacks and queues together as the basic building blocks kernel code reaches for before anything fancier.

A **deque** (double-ended queue) generalizes both ADTs by allowing push/pop at either end; it is usually implemented as a growable array of fixed-size blocks (CPython's `collections.deque` is a doubly linked list of such blocks) or as a single circular buffer that can grow at either boundary, and it subsumes stacks and FIFO queues as special cases.

Growable-array stacks and queues need a **shrink policy** as well as a grow policy: halving capacity as soon as size drops below half after every doubling causes thrashing (grow, shrink, grow, ...) on an alternating push/pop workload; the standard fix is hysteresis — only shrink once size falls to a quarter of capacity, and then only to half.

Concurrency changes the picture again. A single global lock around a stack or queue is simplest and often fast enough; where it is not, Michael and Scott's two-lock queue keeps a separate lock for the head and the tail (with a dummy node that decouples them), and true lock-free variants use compare-and-swap on the tail pointer instead of any lock. Bounded producer-consumer buffers add blocking instead of failing on empty/full, classically via two counting semaphores (`empty`, `full`) plus a mutex guarding the shared ring buffer.

Real systems: the x86-64 hardware call stack (`push`/`pop`/`call`/`ret` against `%rsp`) backs every procedure's activation record; C++'s `std::stack` and `std::queue` are container adaptors over `std::deque` by default; and breadth-first search replaces Dijkstra's priority queue with a plain FIFO queue when all edge weights are equal, giving $O(V+E)$ instead of $O(E\lg V)$.

complexity.notes: worst case triggers a capacity-doubling copy
no resize needed unless a shrink policy triggers a halving copy
enqueue rejected at size $C$, dequeue rejected at size 0
tail pointer is required or enqueue degrades to $O(n)$
worst case is a one-time transfer of all in-stack elements; amortized via $\Phi = 2|\text{in}|$

code.caption: Fixed-capacity ring buffer using an explicit size counter to disambiguate head == tail; the main() run exercises a full wraparound.

worked_example.problem: Trace the two-stack queue (`in`, `out`) through `enqueue(1)`, `enqueue(2)`, `enqueue(3)`, `dequeue()`, `enqueue(4)`, `dequeue()`, `dequeue()`, `dequeue()`. For each step give the actual number of primitive stack operations, the potential $\Phi = 2\,|\text{in}|$ before and after, and the amortized cost $\text{actual} + \Delta\Phi$. Confirm the dequeued values come out in FIFO order and that the amortized costs are all $O(1)$.
worked_example.solution:
| Step | Operation | `in` before → after | `out` before → after | Actual | $\Phi$ before | $\Phi$ after | Amortized |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | enqueue(1) | [] → [1] | [] → [] | 1 | 0 | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | enqueue(2) | [1] → [1,2] | [] → [] | 1 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| 3 | enqueue(3) | [1,2] → [1,2,3] | [] → [] | 1 | 4 | 6 | 3 |
| 4 | dequeue() → 1 | [1,2,3] → [] | [] → [3,2] | 7 | 6 | 0 | 1 |
| 5 | enqueue(4) | [] → [4] | [3,2] → [3,2] | 1 | 0 | 2 | 3 |
| 6 | dequeue() → 2 | [4] → [4] | [3,2] → [3] | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| 7 | dequeue() → 3 | [4] → [4] | [3] → [] | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| 8 | dequeue() → 4 | [4] → [] | [] → [] | 3 | 2 | 0 | 1 |

Step 4 is the expensive one: `in` has 3 elements, so the transfer pops all 3 from `in` and pushes all 3 onto `out` ($3+3=6$ primitive ops), then one more pop from `out` returns the front value — $6+1=7$ actual operations, matching $\Theta(k)$ for $k=3$. Its potential drops from $6$ to $0$, so the amortized cost is $7 + (0-6) = 1$.

Step 8 repeats the pattern with $k=1$: actual cost $2(1)+1=3$, $\Delta\Phi = 0-2=-2$, amortized $3-2=1$.

The dequeued values are $1, 2, 3, 4$ — exactly the enqueue order, confirming FIFO behavior. Every amortized cost in the table is $1$ or $3$, i.e. $O(1)$, and the total actual cost ($1+1+1+7+1+1+1+3=16$) equals the total amortized cost ($3+3+3+1+3+1+1+1=16$), as it must since $\Phi$ starts and ends at $0$ and the two sums differ only by the telescoping $\sum \Delta\Phi = \Phi_{\text{final}} - \Phi_{\text{initial}} = 0$.

pitfalls: Comparing only `head == tail` on a ring buffer without a size counter, wasted slot, or sticky flag makes empty and full indistinguishable.
Transferring only part of `in` onto `out` during a two-stack dequeue breaks FIFO order — a transfer must move every element before any pop from `out`.
Halving a growable array's capacity immediately whenever size drops below half thrashes between growing and shrinking on an alternating push/pop workload; shrink only once size falls to a quarter.
Forgetting to reset `tail` to `NULL` when a linked queue's last node is dequeued leaves a dangling tail pointer that corrupts the next enqueue.
Evaluating postfix `a b -` by popping the first value as the left operand computes $b - a$ instead of the correct $a - b$; the second-popped value is always the left operand.
applications: OS process scheduling: the ready queue and each device's wait queue link PCBs directly through a pointer field inside every PCB — a linked-queue representation, because a process leaving a wait queue must be removed without shifting the others.

Device-driver ring buffers: fixed capacity, sized to a power of two so index wraparound is a mask instead of a modulo, giving a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer channel between interrupt and process context.
The x86-64 hardware call stack: `push`/`pop`/`call`/`ret` against `%rsp` back every procedure's activation record and its return address.
C++ STL: `std::stack` and `std::queue` are container adaptors, backed by `std::deque` by default rather than by a raw array or linked list.

OS bounded buffers: the producer-consumer problem guards a fixed-capacity ring buffer with counting semaphores (`empty`, `full`) and a mutex; Michael and Scott's two-lock queue relaxes a single global lock into separate head/tail locks for higher concurrent throughput.
Graph BFS: replacing Dijkstra's priority queue with a plain FIFO queue on unit-weight graphs turns shortest-path computation into $O(V+E)$ breadth-first search.

self_check.question: A singly linked list gives $O(1)$ push/pop for a stack using only a head pointer, but a singly linked queue needs an explicit tail pointer to get $O(1)$ enqueue. Why the difference, and where exactly would an implementation without a tail pointer lose its $O(1)$ bound?
self_check.answer: A stack's `push` and `pop` always touch the same end of the list (the head), so a single head pointer is sufficient to locate the node either operation needs in $O(1)$. A queue's `enqueue` and `dequeue` touch *opposite* ends: `dequeue` removes the head, but `enqueue` must append after the last node. Without a maintained `tail` pointer, finding that last node requires walking the list from the head, which costs $\Theta(n)$ for a list of $n$ elements — every single enqueue, not just an occasional one, so there is no amortization to appeal to. Keeping a `tail` pointer fixes this, but it introduces its own bookkeeping: when the last remaining node is dequeued, `tail` must be reset to `NULL` (or to the sentinel), or the next enqueue will link a new node after a node that is no longer part of the list.

self_check.question: Using the two-stack queue with potential $\Phi = 2\,|\text{in}|$, trace `enqueue(a)`, `enqueue(b)`, `dequeue()`, `enqueue(c)`, `dequeue()`, `dequeue()`. Give the actual cost, $\Delta\Phi$, and amortized cost of each step, and check that the total actual cost equals the total amortized cost.
self_check.answer:
| Step | Operation | `in` | `out` | Actual | $\Delta\Phi$ | Amortized |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | enqueue(a) | [] → [a] | [] | 1 | +2 | 3 |
| 2 | enqueue(b) | [a] → [a,b] | [] | 1 | +2 | 3 |
| 3 | dequeue() → a | [a,b] → [] | [] → [b] | 5 | −4 | 1 |
| 4 | enqueue(c) | [] → [c] | [b] | 1 | +2 | 3 |
| 5 | dequeue() → b | [c] | [b] → [] | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 6 | dequeue() → c | [c] → [] | [] | 3 | −2 | 1 |

Step 3 transfers $k=2$ elements: $2k+1=5$ actual operations (pop $b$, pop $a$, push $b$, push $a$ onto `out`, then pop `out`) returning $a$ first, as FIFO order requires. Step 6 transfers $k=1$: $2(1)+1=3$ actual operations, returning $c$. The dequeued order is $a, b, c$, matching the enqueue order. Total actual cost is $1+1+5+1+1+3=12$; total amortized cost is $3+3+1+3+1+1=12$ — equal, because $\Phi$ is $0$ both before the first operation and after the last, so $\sum \Delta\Phi = 0$ and the two totals must agree.

self_check.question: You are writing a device driver where an interrupt handler produces bytes and a process-context thread consumes them (single producer, single consumer). The interrupt handler cannot allocate memory or block on a lock. Which of the representations discussed (growable array, linked list, fixed ring buffer) fits, and what specific ordering guarantee do the producer and consumer need around the shared index variables?
self_check.answer: A fixed-capacity ring buffer is the only fit: it needs no allocation after initialization (ruling out a linked list, which allocates a node per element, and a growable array, which reallocates on resize), and its enqueue/dequeue are $O(1)$ worst case with no blocking. Sizing the capacity to a power of two turns index wraparound into a bitmask instead of a modulo, which matters on a hot interrupt path. Because there is exactly one producer and one consumer, no lock is needed at all if each side only ever writes its own index: the producer writes data into `buf[tail]` and then publishes the new `tail`; the consumer reads `head`, reads `buf[head]`, and then publishes the new `head`. The ordering guarantee that matters is that each side's data write must be visible to the other side *before* the corresponding index update is visible — otherwise the consumer could read a slot the producer has claimed but not yet filled. On a weakly-ordered architecture this requires an explicit memory barrier (a write barrier before publishing `tail`, a read barrier before consuming data at `head`) rather than relying on the compiler or CPU to preserve program order.

key_points: Stack = LIFO; queue = FIFO — both are the same sequence, accessed at one end vs. at two ends.
Array push/pop is O(1) amortized with dynamic growth; linked stack push/pop is O(1) worst case.
A linked queue needs an explicit tail pointer, or enqueue degrades to O(n) per call.
Ring buffers disambiguate head == tail with a size counter, a wasted slot, or a sticky full flag.
Two stacks give a queue with O(1) amortized dequeue, proved via the potential Φ = 2|in|.
Postfix evaluation pops the two most recent operands; the second-popped one is the left operand.
tagline: One sequence, two disciplines: LIFO stacks and FIFO queues, built from arrays, linked lists, ring buffers, or two stacks glued together.
tldr: A stack restricts access to one end (LIFO); a queue splits access across two ends (FIFO). Both are realized as bounded or growable arrays, singly or doubly linked lists, or fixed-capacity **ring buffers** that must disambiguate `head == tail` between empty and full. A queue can also be built from two stacks with $O(1)$ amortized cost per operation, proved with the potential method, and the same stack discipline underlies postfix expression evaluation and the shunting-yard algorithm.
